beats.caption: A tariff is a tax paid at the border
beats.text: A tariff is an import tax charged when goods cross into a country. The importer of record pays it to customs, not the foreign seller, so a US server maker importing boards from Asia writes the check.

beats.caption: Section 301 and 232 tariffs raise hardware costs
beats.text: Section 301 tariffs hit many Chinese-made goods, and Section 232 national-security actions cover steel, aluminum and are being used to probe semiconductors. A 25% duty on a $10,000 part adds $2,500 to the landed cost of every unit.

beats.caption: Companies move assembly to avoid the duty
beats.text: Tariffs depend on country of origin, so server and electronics makers shift final assembly to Mexico, Taiwan, Vietnam or Thailand. Moving a line takes quarters and capex, but can cut the duty to near zero under trade deals.

beats.caption: Deadlines pull orders forward
beats.text: When a new tariff is announced with a start date, buyers rush to import before it hits. That inflates revenue and inventory for a quarter or two, then demand can dip after the deadline.

beats.caption: Filings show it in gross margin and risk factors
beats.text: Companies either absorb the duty, which shrinks gross margin, or pass it on in prices, which can hurt volume. Look for tariff lines in risk factors and margin guidance. Related: Dell (DELL), Super Micro (SMCI), Apple (AAPL), Applied Materials (AMAT), Celestica (CLS).
